\chapter{Numbers One to Ten}
\label{ch:ml-numbers-one-to-ten}
\hlchaptermodality{7}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can hear, say, read, and write representative numbers from one to ten in Malayalam.}

Count onnu to pathu, read the ten numeral shapes out of order, and write ezhu with its numeral from sound alone.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[onnu randu moonnu naalu anchu]{One to five — voice first}

\label{lesson:ML-C07-numbers-1-5}



\begin{quote}
This lesson has no Malayalam writing to decode. Hear the five words, attach each one to a quantity, and say them before your eyes meet the script.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{quantity} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
1 & \emph{\textbf{onnu}} \\
2 & \emph{\textbf{randu}} \\
3 & \emph{\textbf{moonnu}} \\
4 & \emph{\textbf{naalu}} \\
5 & \emph{\textbf{anchu}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Point to one finger and say \emph{onnu}. Add one finger at a time: \emph{randu, moonnu, naalu, anchu}. {[}REPEAT x2{]}
\end{sounds}

\begin{culture}
Malayalam and Tamil were once one language, and the family resemblance is still audible. Malayalam \emph{onnu} sits beside Tamil \emph{onru}; \emph{randu} beside \emph{irandu}; \emph{moonnu} beside \emph{moonru}; and \emph{naalu} beside \emph{naanku}. You do not need to learn the Tamil forms. Listen only for the shared bones.
\end{culture}

\begin{culture}
Five moved furthest: an older \emph{aintu} softened toward Malayalam \emph{anchu}. Say \emph{an-chu} slowly, then normally. The sound comes before its spelling.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{onnu, randu, moonnu, naalu, anchu} while raising one more finger
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{moonnu}; YOU SHOW: 3
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{anchu}; YOU SHOW: 5
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count from one to five without looking. Which word means three? (\emph{\textbf{Moonnu.}}) Which one changed furthest from its older Tamil cousin? (\emph{\textbf{Anchu}, five.}) Next, the first three numeral shapes arrive one small step at a time.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[one, two, three]{\ml{൧} · \ml{൨} · \ml{൩} — three numeral shapes}

\label{lesson:ML-W07-digits-1-3}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{onnu, randu, moonnu}. You already own the meanings and sounds; this lesson adds only their three numeral shapes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{൧}} means 1: \emph{onnu}.
  \item \textbf{\ml{൨}} means 2: \emph{randu}.
  \item \textbf{\ml{൩}} means 3: \emph{moonnu}.
\end{itemize}

Point in order, then out of order: \textbf{\ml{൩} \ml{൧} \ml{൨}}.

\subsection*{Writing — observe and trace}
Keep the models visible. Finger-trace \textbf{\ml{൧}}, \textbf{\ml{൨}}, and \textbf{\ml{൩}} once each. Say the number word only after your finger stops. Do not copy from memory yet.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Point to \textbf{\ml{൨}} and say it. (\emph{\textbf{Randu.}}) Which shape means three? (\textbf{\ml{൩}}.) How many new shapes arrived? (\textbf{Three.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[four, five]{\ml{൪} · \ml{൫} — finish the first five numerals}

\label{lesson:ML-W07-digits-4-5}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ml{൧} \ml{൨} \ml{൩}}. Two shapes remain in the first group.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{൪}} means 4: \emph{naalu}.
  \item \textbf{\ml{൫}} means 5: \emph{anchu}.
\end{itemize}

Now point through \textbf{\ml{൧} \ml{൨} \ml{൩} \ml{൪} \ml{൫}}. The first five numeral shapes are complete.

\subsection*{Writing — observe and trace}
Keep both models visible. Trace \textbf{\ml{൪}} once and \textbf{\ml{൫}} once. Then circle the one you hear: {[}YOU HEAR: \emph{anchu}{]}. (\textbf{\ml{൫}}.)

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which shape means four? (\textbf{\ml{൪}}.) Read \textbf{\ml{൫}}. (\emph{\textbf{Anchu.}}) How many new shapes did this lesson add? (\textbf{Two.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[independent o]{\ml{ഒ} — one new letter unlocks five familiar words}

\label{lesson:ML-W07-number-words-1-5}



\begin{quote}
Say one to five, then read their numerals: \textbf{\ml{൧} \ml{൨} \ml{൩} \ml{൪} \ml{൫}}. The words themselves need only one letter you have not met.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\textbf{\ml{ഒ}} is independent short \emph{o}. It begins \textbf{\ml{ഒന്ന്}}, \emph{onnu}, one.

Every other shape in this row is already familiar:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{numeral} & \textbf{word} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{൧}} & \textbf{\ml{ഒന്ന്}} & \emph{onnu} \\
\textbf{\ml{൨}} & \textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്}} & \emph{randu} \\
\textbf{\ml{൩}} & \textbf{\ml{മൂന്ന്}} & \emph{moonnu} \\
\textbf{\ml{൪}} & \textbf{\ml{നാല്}} & \emph{naalu} \\
\textbf{\ml{൫}} & \textbf{\ml{അഞ്ച്}} & \emph{anchu} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{Writing — observe and trace}
Trace \textbf{\ml{ഒ}} once with its model visible. Then point from \textbf{\ml{൧}} to \textbf{\ml{ഒന്ന്}} and say \emph{onnu}. Read the remaining four rows; do not copy the whole row yet.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which new letter begins \emph{onnu}? (\textbf{\ml{ഒ}}.) Read \textbf{\ml{൩}} and \textbf{\ml{മൂന്ന്}}. (\emph{\textbf{Moonnu}, three.}) How many new letters appeared? (\textbf{One.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[one to five]{\ml{൧} \ml{൨} \ml{൩} \ml{൪} \ml{൫} — one visible copy}

\label{lesson:ML-W07-numbers-1-5-guided-copy}

\label{lesson:ML-W07-numbers-1-5-delayed-copy}

\section[one to five]{Three heard numbers — write their numerals}

\label{lesson:ML-W07-numbers-1-5-dictation}



\begin{quote}
Cover the answer line. You will hear familiar words, never an untaught form.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — dictation}
{[}YOU HEAR: \emph{randu — anchu — moonnu}{]}

Write the three numeral shapes from sound alone. Then uncover and compare: \textbf{\ml{൨} \ml{൫} \ml{൩}}. Repair one shape if needed; do not rewrite the whole line.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Write the numeral for \emph{naalu} from sound alone. (\textbf{\ml{൪}}.) You are now ready to hear six through ten before meeting any of their shapes.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aaru ezhu ettu ompathu pathu]{Six to ten — voice first}

\label{lesson:ML-C07-numbers-6-10}



\begin{quote}
Count \emph{onnu} through \emph{anchu}. Keep your pencil down: the next five meanings and sounds come before their shapes.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{quantity} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
6 & \emph{\textbf{aaru}} \\
7 & \emph{\textbf{ezhu}} \\
8 & \emph{\textbf{ettu}} \\
9 & \emph{\textbf{ompathu}} \\
10 & \emph{\textbf{pathu}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say the row once slowly, then once at counting speed. {[}REPEAT x2{]}
\end{sounds}

\begin{culture}
The middle sound of \emph{ezhu} is the curled \textbf{zh} heard in the name \emph{Tamil} in its native form. Malayalam and Tamil kept it; Kannada and Telugu hardened it. Practise only the sound now: \emph{e-zhu}. The written letter waits for a later micro-lesson.
\end{culture}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Ompathu} grew from an old word for \textbf{one} plus \emph{pathu}, \textbf{ten}: one short of ten. Before \emph{p}, the older \emph{n} becomes \emph{m}. Say \emph{on-pathu} slowly, then let it settle into \emph{ompathu}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aaru, ezhu, ettu, ompathu, pathu}
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{ezhu}; YOU SHOW: 7
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{ompathu}; YOU SHOW: 9
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count six to ten. Which word preserves the rare \emph{zh}? (\emph{\textbf{Ezhu.}}) How is \emph{ompathu} built? (\textbf{One plus ten: one short of ten.}) Next, the numeral shapes arrive in groups of three or fewer.
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[virama]{\ml{◌്} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S02-sign-virama}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{ക} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{◌്}}
\textbf{\ml{◌്}} — \emph{no sound of its own — it takes one away}.

It is a \textbf{vowel-killer}. Every consonant in this script arrives with an \emph{a} already inside it — that is what an abugida is. This mark takes the \emph{a} back, leaving the bare consonant. It is how the script writes two consonants in a row.

You already say these, and every one of them has \ml{◌്} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{നമസ്കാരം}} \emph{namaskāram} — hello / greetings (namaskāram — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\ml{നന്ദി}} \emph{nandi} — thank you
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഇല്ല}} \emph{illa} — no / there isn't (illa — the negative)
  \item \textbf{\ml{പേര്}} \emph{pēr} — name
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{◌്} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ml{◌്} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ml{◌്} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ml{നമസ്കാരം}  ·  \ml{നന്ദി}  ·  \ml{ശരി}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ml{◌്} three times, and each time say what it does: \textbf{it kills the built-in \emph{a}}
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ml{◌്} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ml{◌്}? What does it do to the consonant it sits on? (\textbf{Takes away the built-in \emph{a}.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[va]{\ml{വ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S110-letter-va}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{ര} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{വ}}
\textbf{\ml{വ}} — \emph{va}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{v}, it is \textbf{va}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \ml{വ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{പോയി} \ml{വരാം}} \emph{pōyi varāṁ} — goodbye (lit. \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\ml{വീണ്ടും} \ml{കാണാം}} — we'll meet again
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{വ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ml{വ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ml{വ} in the ones that have it

\begin{quote}
\ml{നമസ്കാരം}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ml{വ} three times, saying \emph{va} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ml{വ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
